Searching for superconductivity in doped triangular lattice Kitaev magnets

Preprint: APS/123-QED
Andrew Hardy Thanks: andrew.hardy@mail.utoronto.ca Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, 60 St. George Street, Toronto, ON, M5S 1A7 Canada    Ryan Levy Thanks: Current affiliation: PsiQuantum, 700 Hansen Way, Palo Alto, CA 94304, USA Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, New York, New York 10010, USA    Arun Paramekanti Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, 60 St. George Street, Toronto, ON, M5S 1A7 Canada
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Motivated by exploring correlated metals with frustrating bond-dependent exchange interactions, we study hole and electron doped Kitaev Mott insulators on the triangular lattice. Using homogeneous parton mean field theory, we find that the stripe antiferromagnetic (AFM) order for Kitaev coupling K>0K>0 and the ferromagnetic (FM) order for K<0K<0, both vanish at sufficiently large doping, beyond which we find regimes with chiral d±i​dd\pm id singlet pairing and p±i​pp\pm ip triplet pairing respectively. Our tensor network computations however reveal that the superconducting correlations are strongly suppressed; while FM order stubbornly persists for the doped K<0K<0 model, the doped K>0K>0 model features emergent spin-charge modulated stripe orders. At higher hole doping for K>0K>0, where AFM order is more strongly suppressed than for the electron doped case, incorporating a sufficiently strong nearest-neighbor attraction yields evidence for singlet dd-wave superconductivity with Luttinger parameter Ksc<1K_{\rm sc}<1. Our work sets the stage for a broader exploration of doping effects in triangular lattice magnets such as NaRuO2 which feature bond-dependent exchange interactions.

Introduction.— Doping correlated magnetic insulators has long been considered a viable path to achieve high-temperature superconductivity (SC) since the discovery of the cuprate superconductors [1, 2, 3, 4]. Based on the picture of resonating valence bond singlets in a Mott insulator as blocked Cooper pairs, parent quantum spin liquids [5, 6] have been a favorite hunting ground for emergent SC upon doping which enables Cooper pair mobility. Stabilizing a parent quantum spin liquid requires spin exchange frustration in the Mott insulator which may be induced by lattice geometry [7], multispin interactions near the Mott transition [8, 9], or bond-dependent interactions from spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as exemplified by the honeycomb Kitaev spin model [10, 11, 12]. This has opened up the broad search for SC in doped Mott insulators where lattice geometry and unconventional spin interactions conspire to induce pairing.

For the honeycomb lattice Kitaev model, relevant to a wide class of spin-orbit coupled Mott insulators such as Na2IrO3, Li2IrO3, and α\alpha-RuCl3 [11, 12, 13], the nature of the ground state induced by doping has proven difficult to determine. While parton mean-field theory (MFT) approaches suggested that the doped Kitaev spin liquid could be an unconventional superconductor [14, 15, 16, 17], tensor network studies show that the doped ferromagnetic (FM) Kitaev model displays enhanced Nagaoka-like ferromagnetism with no signs of SC [18]. The doped antiferromagnetic (AFM) Kitaev model shows an exponential decay of all superconducting correlations, although pair-density waves appear as the leading pairing channel correlations [19, 20]. Frustrated triangular lattice magnets have also long been explored for unconventional SC upon doping [21, 22, 23]. This has been inspired in part by early results of superconductivity in Na1-xCoO2 [24, 25]. Remarkably, experiments on Sn/Si(111) have found evidence for chiral d±i​dd\pm id SC [26] on the triangular lattice, which appears to be captured by nonlocal extensions of dynamical mean field theory [27, 26]. Tensor network studies of superconductivity in the triangular lattice also find that pairing only occurs in the presence of additional frustration or longer-range interactions [28, 29, 30, 31, 32]. These examples highlight the importance of advanced computational algorithms to complement mean field studies of strongly correlated electronic Hamiltonians.

In this Letter, we explore the electronic ground state resulting from doped mobile charge carriers in the triangular lattice Kitaev model. The triangular lattice Kitaev spin model has a magnetically ordered ground state, exhibiting FM order for Kitaev exchange K<0K<0 and stripe AFM order for K>0K>0 [33]. On the materials front, a stripe-ordered ground state driven by bond-anisotropic exchanges has been recently discovered in CsCeSe2{\mathrm{CsCeSe}}_{2} [34]. Such bond-anisotropic terms also appear in descriptions of rare earth magnets such as YbMgGaO4 and related materials [35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 33], as well as in the more recently studied ruthenate NaRuO2 [43, 44, 45] which features jeff=1/2j_{\text{eff}}=1/2 moments from the Ru d5d^{5} configuration coupled via an AFM Kitaev exchange term [43, 44, 45] in addition to other exchange interactions. However, the broad phenomenology of doped Kitaev magnets on the triangular lattice has not been explored to the best of our knowledge, making it an important model to explore the impact of doping.

Here, we study the doped triangular lattice Kitaev model using parton MFT [46] and tensor network computations using variationally uniform matrix product states (VUMPS) [47, 48] which provides the thermodynamic ground-state of the quantum system in a quasi one-dimensional regime. Our parton MFT shows that magnetic order of the Mott insulator persists up to a critical doping, beyond which the ground state is an unconventional dd-wave singlet (K>0K>0) or pp-wave triplet (K<0K<0) superconductor. By contrast, while our VUMPS simulations confirm the magnetic orders found in MFT at half-filling, they instead show that the doped state exhibits persistent FM order (K<0K<0) or emergent spin-charge stripe orders (K>0K>0) which strongly suppresses pairing. These spin-charge coupled stripe orders found in our work appear as holes doped into antiphase domain walls in the parent stripe AFM order.

Upon further doping, we find that the spin stripe order is lost, giving way to a non-superconducting state with a spin gap but no charge gap. This raises the intriguing possibility that this regime in the 22D limit could potentially be a fractionalized algebraic charge liquid with gapped bosonic spinons and mobile fermionic holons [49].

Since our VUMPS simulations show that superconductivity seems to be absent in the pure doped Kitaev model, we analyze the impact of an additional nearest-neighbor attractive interaction, possibly induced by phonons. For a sufficiently strong attractive interaction, we find evidence for induced dd-wave pairing. Our results may have broader implications for phonon-induced long-range attraction [50, 51, 52] which could be relevant to extended Hubbard models for moiré transition metal dichalcogenides [53, 54], and experiments on such materials [55]. Our work highlights the importance of newly developed numerical VUMPS algorithms, demonstrating its strengths and value in complementing MFT with careful studies of SC and competing orders in strongly correlated electronic systems with gapless phases.

Model Hamiltonian. The physics of doped Mott insulators relies on the competition between magnetic exchanges and kinetic energy. We begin with the Kitaev spin model on the triangular lattice in the undoped limit

HK=K​∑⟨𝐫,𝐫′⟩Sμ𝐫𝐫′​(𝐫)​Sα𝐫𝐫′​(𝐫′)\begin{gathered}H_{K}=K\sum_{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rangle}S^{\mu_{\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}}(\mathbf{r})S^{\alpha_{\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\end{gathered} (1)

with μ𝐫𝐫′={x,y,z}\mu_{\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}=\{x,y,z\} for the three bond directions. These directions are x^=(12,−32),y^=(12,32),and ​z^=(1,0)\hat{x}\!=\!(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}),\hat{y}\!=\!(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}),\textrm{and }\hat{z}\!=\!(1,0). The classical ground state for K>0K>0 is a nematic with broken spin-lattice rotation symmetry, featuring pockets of stripe AFM order along various directions without long-range magnetic order [56]. The K<0K<0 classical ground state lies at the boundary of FM and stripe AFM orders [56]. In the quantum limit, previous studies considered the possibility of a chiral spin liquid phase for the K>0K>0 case [57], although recent consensus is that the ground state is magnetically ordered: a period-2 stripe AFM for K>0K>0 and a ferromagnet for K<0K<0 [58, 35, 33, 59].

To include mobile charge carriers in the system, we introduce an isotropic kinetic hopping term parameterized by tt terms, as a generalization of the tt-JJ model.

H=−t∑⟨𝐫,𝐫′⟩𝒫(c†𝐫,αc𝐫′,α+h.c.)𝒫+HK,\begin{gathered}H=-t\sum_{{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rangle}}\mathcal{P}\left(c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\alpha}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)\mathcal{P}+H_{K},\end{gathered} (2)

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the Gutwziller projection that projects out doubly occupied sites to account for the large local Hubbard repulsion. We fix t=1t=1 and tune the ratio K/tK/t and dopant concentration δ=1−n\delta=1-n, with δ>0\delta>0 and δ<0\delta<0 corresponding to hole and electron doping respectively.

Parton Mean Field Theory.— To gain a qualitative picture of the stability of the magnetic states or the possibility of novel charge states, we consider a homogeneous parton mean-field theory of the tt-KK model. We consider a parton decomposition, otherwise known as slave-boson theory [46], c𝐫,σ†=b𝐫​f𝐫,σ†c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{r},\sigma}=b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}}f^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{r},\sigma}, with the spin operator then represented as Sμ​(𝐫)=12​f𝐫​α†​σα​βμ​f𝐫′​βS^{\mu}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}\alpha}\sigma_{\alpha\beta}^{\mu}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\beta}. The details of the implementation are presented in the appendix.

The mean field results demonstrate several striking phases shown in Fig. 1. At zero doping, we recover the FM or stripe AFM order. Upon doping with holes or electrons, the magnetic orders remain robust, and persist up to a critical doping δc=γ​|K|/t\delta_{c}=\gamma|K|/t with γ≈0.15\gamma\approx 0.15-0.20.2. At the boundaries of these magnetic phases, for both hole and electron doping, we find emergent topological SC, with (d+i​d)(d+id) singlet for K>0K>0 and (p+ip)|↑↑+↓↓⟩(p+ip)|\uparrow\uparrow+\downarrow\downarrow\rangle triplet for K<0K<0. These superconducting results are consistent with earlier work [57], although we include the possibility of competing magnetic orders, which was not previously considered. Details of the pairing state are given in the appendix. Over the indicated doping range, the phase diagram exhibits only weak particle-hole asymmetry which we attribute to the asymmetry of the density of states on the triangular lattice. These results provide a fascinating example of emergent topological SC at the boundary of frustrated magnetic states, and warrant further investigation using numerical techniques capable of handling the strong correlation constraint.

Variational Uniform Matrix Product States.—

To determine the validity of the parton MFT SC state, we explore the undoped and weakly doped ground state using variational uniform matrix product states. Similar to the infinite-density matrix renormalization group (iDMRG), the VUMPS algorithm performs a variational search over a space of quantum wave functions represented by a uniform matrix product states (UMPS) which capture the thermodynamic limit in the longitudinal direction. We find that finite DMRG tests on the triangular lattice suffer from severe finite size and boundary effects, which motivates studying the system in the infinite limit. Calculations in the thermodynamic limit also have several practical and conceptual advantages in computing quantities such as the transfer matrix and correlation functions [60, 47, 48]. The VUMPS algorithm optimizes directly rather than using a self-consistent ‘bath’ routine like iDMRG, which has been shown to speed up convergence in gapless systems [47, 61]. Details about the algorithmic implementation are in the appendix.

Using VUMPS, we have explored several cuts in the phase diagram from Fig. 1 for hole and electron doping and both signs of KK. Commensurability within the unit cell limits our explored doping values to δ=±1/9,±2/9\delta=\pm 1/9,\pm 2/9 for computationally accessible 1818-site unit cells. We have studied both 9×29\times 2 and 6×36\times 3 unit cells, but we focus here on results in the latter geometry (see Fig.2) as it is more representative of the 2D limit. As these system geometries remain in the quasi-11D limit where MPS methods remain effective, we report the direct ground state without extrapolating to the full 22D thermodynamic limit. To characterize the spin and charge orders, we compute ⟨Sμ​(𝐫)⟩\langle S^{\mu}(\mathbf{r})\rangle and ⟨n⁡(𝐫)⟩\langle n(\mathbf{r})\rangle as well as the connected correlations ⟨Sμ​(𝐫)​Sμ​(𝟎)⟩c≡⟨Sμ​(𝐫)​Sμ​(𝟎)⟩−⟨Sμ​(𝐫)⟩​⟨Sμ​(𝟎)⟩\langle S^{\mu}(\mathbf{r})S^{\mu}{({\bf 0})}\rangle^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{c}\equiv\langle S^{\mu}(\mathbf{r})S^{\mu}({\bf 0})\rangle-\langle S^{\mu}(\mathbf{r})\rangle\langle S^{\mu}(\bf 0)\rangle and ⟨n⁡(𝐫)​n​(𝟎)⟩c≡⟨n⁡(𝐫)​n​(𝟎)⟩−⟨n⁡(𝐫)⟩​⟨n⁡(𝟎)⟩\langle n(\mathbf{r})n({\bf 0})\rangle^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{c}\equiv\langle n(\mathbf{r})n({\bf 0})\rangle-\langle n(\mathbf{r})\rangle\langle n({\bf 0})\rangle. To compute the spin and charge order, we provide a weak symmetry breaking Weiss field along SzS^{z} at a single site which is reduced to zero in the initial sweeps (with bond dimension χ<64\chi<64) of the variational search which provide an ordering preference. We confirm that the undoped model has stripe-AFM order for K>0K>0 and FM order for K<0K<0.

For nonzero dopings we have explored, we find that the ground state for K<0K<0 is a uniform FM metal with strongly suppressed pair correlations. We present pertinent results for that case in the Supplemental Material (SM) [62]. We focus below on results for K>0K>0, where we find emergent spin-charge orders and non-magnetic metallic states which might support SC.

Weak doping of Kitaev AFM, δ=±1/9\delta=\pm 1/9.— As shown in the lower panels and insets of Figs. 2 (a) and (b), a spin-charge stripe order emerges from weak doping of the Kitaev Mott insulator. In the hole-doped case, Fig 2(a), the spin order has wavevector 𝐐sp≡(Q1,Q2)=(π,2​π/3){{\bf{Q}}}_{\rm sp}\equiv(Q_{1},Q_{2})=(\pi,2\pi/3), leading to charge modulation at 𝐐ch=2​𝐐sp=(0,4​π/3){{\bf{Q}}}_{\rm ch}=2{{\bf{Q}}}_{\rm sp}=(0,4\pi/3). This strong charge modulation has a ∼10%\sim 10\% reduction in the charge density in the central leg of the three-leg cylinder. In addition, we find a weaker ≲1%\lesssim 1\% charge modulation along the legs, with a wavelength equal to the unit cell, indicative of universal quasi-1D Luttinger charge-density-wave (CDW) behavior [63]. The electron-doped case, Fig 2(b), also exhibits spin-charge stripes, with a distinct wavevector 𝐐sp=(2​π/3,0){{\bf{Q}}}_{\rm sp}=(2\pi/3,0) and charge modulation at 𝐐ch=2​𝐐sp=(4​π/3,0){{\bf{Q}}}_{\rm ch}=2{{\bf{Q}}}_{\rm sp}=(4\pi/3,0). This leads to every third rung having a strongly depleted charge density as shown, about ∼10%\sim 10\% lower than adjacent rungs. Again, in this case, we observe a weaker superposed quasi-1D charge modulation along the legs. In a manner similar to the spin-charge stripes seen in various hole-doped cuprates [64, 65, 66], we can view the strong spin-charge stripe orders in the weakly doped Kitaev Mott insulator as ‘rivers of charge’ separating domains of stripe-AFM order. The strength of the spin-stripe states with 𝐐ch=2​𝐐sp{{\bf{Q}}}_{\rm ch}=2{{\bf{Q}}}_{\rm sp} for both hole and electron doping, and their persistence irrespective of the lattice geometries explored, indicate that these are genuine ground state orders potentially likely to persist in 2D, while the quasi-1D modulations should weaken and disappear in the 2D limit [67].

We next turn to the connected spin correlation function ⟨Sμ​(𝐫)​Sμ​(𝟎)⟩c\langle S^{\mu}(\mathbf{r})S^{\mu}({\bf 0})\rangle^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{c} shown in the main panels of Figs. 2 (a) and (b), which inform us about spin fluctuations on top of the ordered state. The electron-doped case exhibits spin fluctuations which do not change much with KK, while the hole-doped case exhibits enhanced spin fluctuations as we decrease KK, hinting at a magnetic critical point at this fixed doping. Upon decreasing the Kitaev coupling from K=0.9K=0.9 to K=0.3K=0.3, the correlation length doubles to nearly 44 unit cells (2424 sites), although we do not access a gapless critical point within our restricted sweep. The gapless regime |K|<0.3\absolutevalue{K}<0.3, however, becomes difficult to converge within VUMPS. The nature of the transition from a gapless Fermi liquid to these spin and charge ordered states warrants further investigation, despite the difficulty of such critical states admitting a MPS representation. Such a magnetic critical point could also be accessed by increasing doping at fixed KK.

Strong doping of Kitaev AFM, δ=±2/9\delta=\pm 2/9.— Upon further doping, as shown in Fig. 3(a), the magnetic order is lost on the hole doped side with δ=2/9\delta=2/9, while a charge modulation persists with the central leg having an ∼10%\sim 10\% depleted charge. This is consistent with charge stripe order without an accompanying spin stripe order. In contrast to an SU(2) invariant spinful Luttinger liquid which exhibits long range power-law spin correlations, the spin correlations in this hole-doped Kitaev metal are strongly suppressed and appear short-ranged 3. On the electron-doped side, for δ=−2/9\delta=-2/9, as seen from Fig. 3(b), the coupled spin-charge modulated stripe order persists, with evidence of enhanced spin fluctuations, so that even higher electron doping is needed to access a magnetic critical point. Intriguingly, at this electron doping value, the residual spin order in the spin-charge stripe is seen to get stronger at smaller KK, highlighting the potential role of Haerter-Shastry type kinetic magnetism [68] in determining the spin ordering and particle-hole asymmetry seen in our numerical results. Previous work [69] in fact also sees stripe order in the strict U=∞U=\infty limit that emerges upon sufficient hole doping of the 120∘120^{\circ} order, due to kinetic magnetism effects.

Pair correlations in doped AFM, δ=2/9\delta=2/9.— We now explore the possibility of unconventional superconductivity in these doped Kitaev-Mott insulators. While the VUMPS calculations are performed in a U(1)(1) charge conservation sector, we can determine the superconducting susceptibility through pair correlation functions. Motivated by our parton MFT results, we compute the singlet pair-correlation function Ps​(𝐫)=⟨Δs†​(𝐫)​Δs​(0)⟩P_{s}(\mathbf{r})=\left\langle\Delta^{\dagger}_{s}(\mathbf{r})\Delta_{s}(0)\right\rangle with the singlet operator Δs†​(𝐫)=(c𝐫,↓†​c𝐫+1,↑†−c𝐫,↑†​c𝐫+1,↓†)/2\Delta_{s}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{r})=(c_{\mathbf{r},\downarrow}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{r}+1,\uparrow}^{\dagger}-c_{\mathbf{r},\uparrow}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{r}+1,\downarrow}^{\dagger})/\sqrt{2}. We have similarly defined and computed triplet pair correlations, Pt​(𝐫)P_{t}(\mathbf{r}), but find that these are much more strongly suppressed for both signs of KK and all dopings; we thus relegate these results to the SM [62].

In quasi-1D systems, competing SC and charge-density wave correlations with power-law decay, and exponentially suppressed spin correlations, are characteristic of Luther-Emery (LE) liquids. These are parametrized by exponents (KρK_{\rho}, KscK_{\rm sc}), with Kρ​Ksc=1K_{\rho}K_{\rm sc}=1, which govern the decay of charge and pair correlators, ⟨n⁡(𝟎)​n​(𝐫)⟩∼r−Kρ\langle n({\bf 0})n({\bf r})\rangle\sim r^{-K_{\rho}} and Ps​(𝐫)∼𝐫−KscP_{s}(\mathbf{r})\sim\mathbf{r}^{-K_{\rm sc}}. We identify the LE liquid as a superconductor when Ksc<1K_{\rm sc}<1. Similar to previous tensor-network studies [70, 28, 29, 19, 32]. We determine KscK_{\rm sc} by fitting Ps​(𝐫)P_{s}(\mathbf{r}) to the form 𝐫−Ksc\mathbf{r}^{-K_{\rm sc}} over a range of rr where it obeys power-law decay, before the finite bond-dimension χ\chi causes an eventual crossover to exponential decay. We find that the LE state at δ=2/9\delta=2/9 hole doping, has Ksc≈1.8K_{\rm sc}\approx 1.8, with a negligible dependence on the Kitaev exchange as seen from Fig. 4(a).

The electron doped state, δ=−2/9\delta=-2/9, has an even more suppressed Ps​(𝐫)P_{s}(\mathbf{r}) as seen from in Fig. 4(b), but increasing the Kitaev coupling leads to a decrease from Ksc≈3K_{\rm sc}\approx 3 to Ksc≈2.5K_{\rm sc}\approx 2.5. Neither state, δ=±2/9\delta=\pm 2/9 is, however, consistent with superconducting order with Ksc<1K_{\rm sc}<1. A possible fate of this hole doped state in 2D is a charge density wave or an algebraic charge liquid, i.e. a spin-gapped holon metal [49]. Going beyond the tt-KK model, we therefore explore whether incorporating a nearest-neighbour attraction term in the Hamiltonian HV=−V∑⟨𝐫𝐫′⟩n𝐫n𝐫′H_{V}=-V\sum_{\langle\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rangle}n_{\mathbf{r}}n_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}} can favor SC. Phonons have been proposed to provide a microscopic origin of such an attractive term in various materials [50, 51, 52]. As seen from Fig.5, KscK_{\rm sc} decreases with increasing V/tV/t, eventually leading to a superconducting state with Ksc≈0.8K_{\rm sc}\approx 0.8 for V/t≈1V/t\approx 1. At these substantial interaction strengths, this superconductivity appears primarily due to the attractive interactions. Nonetheless we can ask whether this SC state inherits any of the anisotropic tendencies from the parent Kitaev magnetic state? Our lattice geometry does not support d+i​dd+id pairing given the reduced point group symmetry. We find, instead, that Ps​(𝐫)P_{s}(\mathbf{r}) has a dd-wave form factor with bond amplitudes [0,+,−,0,+,−][0,+,-,0,+,-] while rotating around a site [71], which is consistent with dd-wave singlet SC in this geometry. Up to the 11D constraints on symmetry, this pairing symmetry is reminiscent of that of the Kitaev SC state emerging from the MFT calculation, although the role of pure attractive interactions [52] from one where Kitaev exchange assists this pairing from attraction is not easy to disentangle. This calls for a more comprehensive study of the SC pairing of a Gutzwiller projected state due to attractive phonon interactions to future work.

Discussion.— We have explored the possibility of SC in the doped Kitaev model on the triangular lattice, a paradigmatic example of a strongly correlated metal with bond-anisotropic exchange interactions. While parton MFT finds large regions of the phase diagram containing topological SC, our tensor network simulations instead uncover emergent spin-charge modulated stripe orders at weak doping which give way to a strongly correlated metal at larger hole doping, with dd-wave SC emerging in the presence of strong additional attractive interactions. These results demonstrate the resilience of spin-stripes, such as seen in [34], upon doping. Future work can better explore the fate of these states upon approaching the 22D thermodynamic limit.

Our study also indicates the importance of kinetic magnetism must be explored in frustrated triangular magnets as well as other lattice geometries [72]. An important future direction would be to extend our study to incorporate all symmetry-allowed exchange terms and further neighbor couplings. Such studies may also benefit from exploring the limit of large t/Kt/K where the kinetic effects may be explored in greater detail. Future work may also refine the boundaries of superconductivity upon improving the initial MPS ansatz with other numerical methods [73] In closing, we suggest that hole doping of triangular magnets with antiferromagnetic Kitaev terms, such as NaRuO2 [43, 44, 45] even if it has other exchange terms, would be of immense value to search for the predicted spin-charge modulated stripes and unconventional superconductivity. This work should also serve as impetus for materials discovery to search for new systems exhibiting dominant bond-anisotropic AFM Kitaev interactions on the triangular lattice.

I Appendices

I.1 Parton Mean-Field Theory

The resulting Hamiltonian after the mean-field decomposition of Eq. 2 is

H=\displaystyle H= ∑⟨𝐫,𝐫′⟩−t(f𝐫,σ†f𝐫′,σb𝐫b𝐫′†+ H.c. )\displaystyle\sum_{{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rangle}}-t\left(f_{\mathbf{r},\sigma}^{\dagger}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\sigma}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}}b_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}^{\dagger}+\text{ H.c. }\right) (3)
+K4∑⟨𝐫,𝐫′⟩[(f𝐫,α†σα​βμf𝐫′,β)(f𝐫,α†σα​βμf𝐫′,β)]\displaystyle+\frac{K}{4}\sum_{{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rangle}}\left[\left(f_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}^{\dagger}\sigma^{\alpha\beta}_{\mu}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\beta}\right)\left(f_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}^{\dagger}\sigma^{\alpha\beta}_{\mu}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime},\beta}\right)\right]
+∑𝐫[λ𝐫(f𝐫,σ†f𝐫,σ+b𝐫†b𝐫+1)−μb𝐫b𝐫†].\displaystyle+\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\left[\lambda_{\mathbf{r}}\left(f_{\mathbf{r},\sigma}^{\dagger}f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r},\sigma}+b_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}}+1\right)-\mu b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}}b_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\right].

with a Lagrange multiplier λ𝐫\lambda_{\mathbf{r}} used to impose the Gutzwiller constraint. At zero temperature, the bosons condense with a condensate expectation value of ⟨b𝐫†​b𝐫+1⟩≈b𝐫≈b𝐫†≈δ\sqrt{\left\langle b^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}+1}\right\rangle}\approx b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}}\approx b_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\approx\sqrt{\delta}. This ansatz remains self consistent when the density order remains uniform. We find this to be true for the 33 and 44 site unit cells we consider here. In this analysis, we neglect possible phase fluctuations of the condensate along with potential gauge fluctuations from this fractionalization procedure. This mean-field treatment of the bosons modifies the kinetic term as t→tf=t⁡⟨b𝐫†​b𝐫+1⟩=t​δt\rightarrow t_{f}=t\left\langle b_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathbf{r}+1}\right\rangle=t\delta. This provides the agreement necessary with the Gutzwiller projection that the initial charge and spinon kinetic energy is zero in the insulating regime.

We retain unbiased Hartree terms for the density and spin orientation at each site as

S¯μ​(𝐫)=⟨f𝐫​α†​σμα​β​f𝐫​β⟩\overline{S}_{\mu}(\mathbf{r})=\langle f_{\mathbf{r}\alpha}^{\dagger}\sigma^{\alpha\beta}_{\mu}f_{\mathbf{r}\beta}\rangle with μ∈I,x,y,z\mu\in{I,x,y,z}, i.e.(n¯​(𝐫)=S¯I​(𝐫))i.e.\left(\overline{n}(\mathbf{r})=\overline{S}_{I}(\mathbf{r})\right), and Fock terms for each bond with χμ​(𝐫)=⟨f𝐫,α†​σμα​β​f𝐫+1,β⟩\chi_{\mu}({\mathbf{r}})=\langle f_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}^{\dagger}\sigma^{\alpha\beta}_{\mu}f_{\mathbf{r}+1,\beta}\rangle. In order to study pairing, we also include decompositions into pairing terms of both singlet and triplet operators, given by Δs​(𝐫)=1/2​f𝐫,α​i​σyα,β​f𝐫+1,β\Delta_{s}({\mathbf{r}})=1/\sqrt{2}f_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}i\sigma^{\alpha,\beta}_{y}f_{\mathbf{r}+1,\beta}, Δt1​(𝐫)=c𝐫,↑​c𝐫+1,↑,Δt2​(𝐫)=c𝐫,↓​c𝐫+1,↓\Delta_{t_{1}}(\mathbf{r})=c_{\mathbf{r},\uparrow}c_{\mathbf{r}+1,\uparrow},\Delta_{t_{2}}(\mathbf{r})=c_{\mathbf{r},\downarrow}c_{\mathbf{r}+1,\downarrow}, and Δt3​(𝐫)=12​(c𝐫,↓​c𝐫+1,↑+c𝐫,↑​c𝐫+1,↓)\Delta_{t_{3}}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(c_{\mathbf{r},\downarrow}c_{\mathbf{r}+1,\uparrow}+c_{\mathbf{r},\uparrow}c_{\mathbf{r}+1,\downarrow}\right). These terms are treated on equal-footing with the regular order parameters. The mean-field theory is then numerically solved using root finders until we arrive at self-consistent solutions.

I.2 VUMPS Details

Due to the entanglement scaling of matrix product states (MPS) [75], the VUMPS algorithm is limited to quasi-one dimensional systems with a finite number of ‘legs’, or ‘width’ in the transverse direction. Within this framework, the space of UMPS for a given bond dimension, χ\chi, is interpreted as a manifold with a corresponding tangent space structure [76]. By considering gradient descent computed in this tangent space, one can devise a variational optimization algorithm to find the UMPS with the lowest energy for a given physical system [47]. As such, the VUMPS algorithm works at fixed bond dimension. In order to increase the bond dimension, we use a controlled bond dimension expansion procedure with the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) [77, 78, 79, 80].

We caution however that as is the case with global variational searches, VUMPS can be sensitive to initial wave-function guesses or become stuck in local minima. All calculations are done on an triangular ‘cylinder’, with periodic (infinite) boundary conditions in the L2L_{2} (L1L_{1}) direction up to a maximum χ=2400\chi=2400. The convergence is done with a Schmidt tolerance ϵSVD=10−5\epsilon_{\mathrm{SVD}}=10^{-5}. This corresponds to the energy converging to Δ​E≤10−9\Delta E\leq 10^{-9}. Tensor network methods when dealing with gapless states effectively gap the state due to a finite bond-dimension, providing signatures of a diverging correlation length. We utilize these insights to perform a scaling fit of the dominate eigenvalue of the transfer matrix ξ=−1/log⁡(ϵ1)\xi=-1/\log(\e_1) as a function of the refinement parameter γ=ϵ1−ϵ2\gamma=\epsilon_{1}-\epsilon_{2} in Fig. 6. Through the procedure detailed in [81], we are able to detail the gapless nature of the δ=2/9\delta=2/9 doped state as the correlation length diverges.
